1.pericope_label: The salutation of Paul, Silvanus and Timothy

schools.summary: Henry notes that the introduction repeats the earlier one exactly and draws from it a warning against preferring novelty of phrase to soundness of doctrine.

Barnes dates the letter to Corinth in late 53 or early 54 on three probabilities and identifies its occasion as the belief that the end was at hand; Ellicott dates it inside the second missionary journey because Silvanus is still present, and joins Robertson in judging that the clause naming the Father and the Lord Jesus belongs here rather than in the first epistle; Robertson adds that the two prepositions distinguish the sphere of the church from the source of its grace.

Clarke reconstructs the report brought back by the bearer of the first letter and then argues at length, against certain learned writers, that the apostles never believed the day of judgment would fall in their own lifetime, since to grant it would destroy their authority everywhere.
Calvin takes the word church to mean not merely an assembly gathered in faith but the building of the Father as well as of Christ.
Chrysostom makes the wish for grace the heart of the greeting and illustrates its power from Joseph, who passed through slavery, false accusation and prison as though untouched.

debates: Whether the apostles themselves expected the return of Christ within their lifetime, which Clarke reports as the opinion of respected writers and rejects as destroying the authority of their whole testimony.

Whether the clause naming God the Father and the Lord Jesus Christ belongs to the salutation of the first epistle, where Ellicott and Robertson both judge it an intrusion though it stands rightly here.
outliers: Clarke argues from the delay implied by the man of sin and by the future ingathering of the Jews that no apostle can have thought the end was near.

3.pericope_label: Thanksgiving for growing faith, and glorying in the churches

schools.summary: Gill grounds the constant thanks in God’s constant giving and distinguishes glorying about men from glorying in them; Calvin makes daily growth the true commendation of believers, argues that thanks for the increase proves the increase is God’s, and makes patience the fruit and evidence of faith.

Ellicott treats the thanksgiving as a debt incurred, calls the verb for growth an enthusiastic word outgrowing all bounds, and defines patience as heroic endurance and persecution as organised hostility distinct from general tribulation; Robertson analyses the compound verb, connects the abounding love to the earlier prayer, and notes a variant reading; Barnes takes the report as evidence that news had come from Thessalonica.

Clarke likens the growth to a well planted tree bearing fruit, insists it was true of every member, and holds that persecution never essentially injured the genuine Church; Wesley observes that Paul wraps his praise of men inside praise of God.

debates: Whether the clause of reason attaches to the thanksgiving or to the words "as it is meet", Ellicott arguing for the latter.
Whether "we glory in you" can stand with the rule against glorying in men, which Gill resolves by referring the glorying to the grace of God in them.
outliers: Robertson reports that the fulfilment here of a prayer made in the earlier letter has been used as evidence for the order of the two epistles.
Ellicott reads the emphatic pronoun as an admission that the writers had themselves harboured misgivings about this church.

5.pericope_label: A manifest token of the righteous judgment of God

schools.summary: Gill rejects the future-looking readings because the apostle speaks of present suffering and settles on the visible inequality of providence; Calvin makes the sufferings of the innocent a mirror of the coming judgment and sets this against the profane conclusion that the world runs by chance.
Henry finds a present advantage in the trials, which prove them Christians indeed, and allows a worthiness of congruity but not of condignity.

Barnes supplies the relative from the whole preceding sentence and makes the manner of enduring an advance indication of the verdict; Ellicott locates the token in the bare fact of persecution, warns against pressing the epithet, and reads "counted worthy" as the sentence itself rather than a question of merit, adding that the saints are counted worthy of the kingdom itself and not merely of entry; Robertson keeps to the syntax and insists the judgment is the final one.

Clarke weighs two readings and prefers the maxim that the sufferings of the just and the triumphs of the wicked prove a judgment to come, allowing a gospel sense of worthiness grounded in bearing the image of God; Wesley refers the token forward to the verses that follow.

debates: What the token is a token of: the whole course of their endurance (Barnes), the bare fact of persecution (Ellicott), the divine rightness of calling the Gentiles or the general maxim of a judgment to come (Clarke), or the present inequality of providence (Gill).
Whether "counted worthy" bears on merit at all, where Henry, Barnes and Clarke each qualify it carefully and Ellicott denies that the question arises.
outliers: Calvin supports the argument with a pagan poet who said the misfortunes of the good tempt him to think there are no gods, and with a tyrant who robbed a temple and took a fair wind home as proof that heaven favours sacrilege.
Ellicott argues that believers are already in the kingdom as subjects and are to be declared worthy of the kingdom itself, to inherit and reign in it.

6.pericope_label: Recompense to the persecutors and rest to the persecuted

schools.summary: Gill distinguishes what is righteous in itself from what men account righteous and weighs a temporary relief from persecution against the final rest, preferring the latter; Calvin argues that without a deferred judgment the government of the world would be unjust, refuses to speculate about the nature of the fire, and makes Paul’s sharing of the trials the credential of his teaching.

Ellicott renders the condition as an appeal to what the readers will grant and argues from the conscience that what is fair among men is fair with God, making the angels the executors of Christ’s power rather than his retinue; Barnes contends at length that future punishment is just and therefore certain, while noting that the reward of the righteous is of grace and not of desert; Robertson stresses that the phrase means right from God’s own standpoint and that the coming is described as an unveiling.

Clarke holds that God gives particular proofs of displeasure against persecutors and describes the attending angels as the court of the judge; Wesley identifies a specific slaughter of Jews at a passover as the beginning of the recompense.

debates: Whether the attending angels form the retinue of the judge, as Clarke has it, or are the agents through whom his power is executed, as Ellicott and Calvin insist.
Whether the promised rest includes present relief from persecution, which Gill entertains before preferring the final rest and which Ellicott denies before the judgment day.
Whether the recompense to the persecutors had already begun in history, as Wesley argues from a contemporary massacre, or belongs wholly to the last day.
outliers: Barnes marks an asymmetry the others pass over: the wicked will deserve all they suffer, but the righteous do not deserve what they receive.

Calvin declines to discuss the nature of the fire, leaving it to persons of foolish curiosity, and pictures Paul as a soldier who fights beside those he instructs rather than directing them from the shade.

8.pericope_label: Flaming fire, vengeance, and everlasting destruction

schools.summary: Gill leaves the fire between Christ and the angels and grounds the endlessness of the punishment in the endlessness of the sin; Calvin asks whether vengeance may lawfully be desired and answers that we must wish well to all while we cannot tell who the wicked are, and proves the perpetuity of the death from its being set opposite the unending glory of Christ.

Ellicott repunctuates so that the fire attends the presence rather than the punishment, denies that the word for vengeance can mean personal revenge, restricts the guilty Gentiles to those whose ignorance was voluntary, reads the destruction as banishment from an oriental court, and concedes that the passages on the last state cannot at present be reconciled; Barnes takes the fire for incessant lightning and argues that if this language does not teach eternal punishment no language could; Robertson traces the phrase to a Maccabean parallel and holds that "age-long" here means the coming age.

Clarke renders the fire as thunder and lightning, extends the disobedient to nominal Christians who will not take the gospel as a rule of life, and confesses he cannot say what the destruction consists in; Wesley grounds its endlessness, as Gill does, in the continuance of the enmity.
Chrysostom answers those who comfort themselves that hell is milder and temporary by pointing to the word everlasting, and observes that the same coming is light to some and vengeance to others.

debates: Whether the flaming fire belongs to the attending angels or to the punishment, Ellicott repunctuating to make it an attribute of the divine presence.
Who the two classes are: Gentiles and Jews by the repeated article (Ellicott, Robertson, Wesley), with Clarke adding nominal Christians to the second.

How confidently the endlessness of the punishment can be asserted from this text, where Barnes says no clearer language is possible and Ellicott allows that two sets of passages resist reconciliation.
outliers: Calvin raises and answers the question whether a Christian may lawfully desire the vengeance the verse promises.
Gill and Wesley, from opposite camps, give the same argument that unending sin requires unending punishment.

10.pericope_label: Glorified in his saints and admired in them that believe

schools.summary: Calvin reads the verse as a promise that the saints will share the glory rather than merely display it, sets it against their present condition of labour and contempt, takes "saints" to be explained by "believers" so that there is no holiness apart from faith, and concludes that God’s promises are ratified in us when they gain credit with us; Gill divides the glory into what Christ shows them and what he bestows on them.

Ellicott makes the glorifying the effect rather than the purpose of the coming, matches the two classes of the saved to the two classes of the punished, and explains the past tense as looking back from the judgment to the moment of decision; Barnes weighs whether Christ is admired by or in his people and settles on the latter, listing what will then be admired and observing that this honour has never yet been seen; Robertson reports both the suggested reason for the tense and another scholar’s verdict that the parenthesis is an anti-climax.

Clarke contrasts the believer’s present admiration of the Redeemer with what he will feel on seeing the glory Christ had before the world was, endorses the past tense as undoubtedly genuine, and proposes that the clauses of the sentence have been transposed; Wesley says only that the glory of Christ shall shine in them.

debates: Whether Christ is admired by those who believe or in them, Barnes weighing both and preferring the second, which Ellicott and Calvin also assume.
What to do with the closing parenthesis, which Clarke would rearrange as transposed, Ellicott explains as an assurance to the readers, and Robertson reports being dismissed as an anti-climax.
outliers: Ellicott aligns the saints and the believers one for one against those who know not God and those who obey not the gospel.
Barnes holds that the chief honour of Christ at his coming will be the redeemed church rather than any outward splendour.

11.pericope_label: The prayer that God would count them worthy of the calling

schools.summary: Calvin refers the calling to the end that depends on perseverance and answers that God must confirm what He began, then presses the phrase about good pleasure into a denial that any merit of ours contributes at any stage; Gill notes that the apostles added prayer to counsel.
Henry makes the expectation of the coming a reason for prayer, insists we must be taught what to ask, and reads the petition as asking God to make us worthy since we have no worthiness of our own.

Ellicott refers the calling to the summons of the last day and warns that the past call is no security of proving worthy of it, declines the common reading that makes the goodness the readers’ own, and assigns the work of faith wholly to God; Robertson allows the calling to mean both beginning and issue and turns the second phrase into a wish that they delight in goodness; Barnes takes the petition plainly and glosses the power as effectual.

Clarke traces the goodness through four stages and states that while the power must come from God the exercise of it must be the believer’s own; Wesley defines the good pleasure of God’s goodness as perfect holiness.

debates: Whether the calling in view is the one already obeyed or the final summons of the judgment day, where Ellicott argues for the last and warns that the earlier call is no security, Calvin refers it to the end but grounds security in God’s confirming, and Robertson allows both senses.

Whose goodness is meant in "the good pleasure of his goodness": God’s, taken almost as a personified beneficence (Ellicott, Calvin, Henry), or the readers’ own moral aspirations, which Ellicott reports as the common modern view and rejects.

How far the believer contributes: Calvin denies that grace is helped along by subsequent merits, while Clarke, on the same phrase, holds that the exercise of the God-given power must be the believer’s own.
outliers: Ellicott, Calvin, Barnes and Robertson all refer the closing "work of faith" to God’s work in the readers rather than to their own activity.

12.pericope_label: That the name of our Lord Jesus Christ may be glorified in you

schools.summary: Calvin declines to explain how the glory belongs to God and Christ in common, calls the mutual glorifying a doubled miracle, and insists that nothing in it is ours; Gill observes that the name is dishonoured by unworthy professors and glorified by faith and patience.

Robertson lays out the argument from the single article that would make the closing words call Jesus our God and Lord, then admits it is not decisive and leaves both renderings open; Ellicott attaches the clause about grace only to the glorifying of the readers and reads the verse as gathering up the preceding paragraph, where lost and saved alike must acknowledge Christ and those who followed Him; Barnes closes with three inferences about the certainty, the eternity and the justice of the punishment.

Clarke makes the magnifying of Christ’s passion the end of the calling, holds that God saves as it becomes God to save, argues that the bare existence of religious persecution disproves any denial of human depravity, and urges preachers to keep eternal destruction before their hearers; Wesley says the love and power of the Lord are to be displayed in them.

debates: Whether the single article at the close makes "our God and the Lord Jesus Christ" one person or two, which Robertson argues both ways and leaves undecided and Calvin expressly declines to discuss here.
Whether the clause about grace governs the whole sentence or only the glorifying of believers in Christ, Ellicott restricting it to the latter.
outliers: Clarke, arguing from the wesleyan side, treats the mere existence of religious persecution as an absolute empirical disproof of any denial of original sin.
Barnes holds that the aggravation of the lost will be their own conviction that the sentence is just, since suffering is bearable only while conscience says it is undeserved.
